title: Hello [Open] World: Unbody Is Now OSS (Alpha)
author: amir
blurb: Unbody announces its transition to open source, releasing an alpha version of its modular, AI-native backend designed to be the 'Supabase of the AI era'. This release prioritizes architectural flexibility, allowing developers to build autonomous agents and complex AI applications with transparent, customizable infrastructure.

summary.summary: Unbody positions itself as the first open, modular backend for the AI-native era.
It is a data knowledge driven, AI-native backend designed to replace traditional stacks.
The system is architected for modularity, autonomous agent support, and plugin extensibility.
They are building the Supabase of the AI era and inviting you to help shape it.
The repository is located at github.com/unbody-io/unbody.
When they launched Unbody commercially last year, one truth became clear after experimenting with curiosity and grit.
But one truth became clear: We weren’t going to build an excellent product without involving the wider developer community in the process.
We're releasing Unbody as open source because we believe it's the best way to build a better product and gain developer adoption.
Open source allows for inspection, customization, and local deployment, which are critical for building trust in intelligent systems.
This alpha release focuses on architectural flexibility and modularity rather than feature completeness.
The modular design supports both traditional plugins and autonomous AI agents that can process information.
The Contextual Data Engine is built to transform raw, fragmented data into structured, queryable knowledge.
The architecture supports connections to tools like Unstructured.io and LlamaIndex.
Our open-source version already outclasses our cloud service in terms of architectural openness and modularity.
Our cloud offering comes with significant trade-offs like locked-in storage and inflexible pipelines.
The open-source version gives you greater flexibility to choose storage solutions and AI models.
Despite significant refactors in data ingestion, our content API remains unchanged.
Our roadmap envisions the eventual replacement of our cloud version with this open-source powerhouse.
We’re sharing Unbody OSS Alpha to open a discussion with the wider community.
The AI tooling ecosystem is scattered and complex, often requiring dozens of decisions.
The authors ask: What if there were a Supabase, but for the AI era?
Supabase radically simplified how we build modern web apps by unifying developer-friendly stacks.
Unbody aims to bring that same spirit to AI-native software intended to reason, adapt, and act.
Supabase is great, but it wasn’t built for a world where your backend needs to think.
Supabase and Firebase are built around storing static data in tables, which is insufficient for AI-native products.
This is because the way we interact with software has fundamentally changed.
Today, we talk to software and expect it to reason, summarize, and take action on our behalf.
AI-native software is active and context-aware, requiring a backend that evolves from storing static data to managing knowledge.
AI-native software needs enriched, connected data that enables reasoning rather than just rows in tables.
To mimic human intelligence, software needs a dynamic, evolving graph of meaning.
Tasks like chunking and vectorization are essential infrastructure, not extras to be duct-taped together.
If software understands like a human, the backend must process images, video, audio, and more.
It’s a Supabase-style stack for building AI-native products from the ground up.
Without Unbody, even building a simple Q&A bot requires complex setup.
It requires spinning up a vector database like Weaviate or Pinecone.
It involves creating a pipeline for chunking and ingesting content.
Developers must stitch all this into their backend and maintain it.
It’s built for opinionated flexibility, allowing you to bring your own vector store or AI provider.
The image displays the Unbody modular stack architecture.
Please see the README.md on our Github repo for more in-depth information and a complete list of modules.
If software is becoming more like humans, then the backend that powers it needs to work like a brain.
Unbody is built on four functional layers: Perception, Memory, Reasoning, and Action.
Perception handles how the system sees and understands the world.
Memory manages what the system knows and remembers.
Reasoning covers how the system thinks, decides, and plans.
Action defines how the system interacts with others and takes initiative.
The Perception layer is where raw data becomes structured, enriched knowledge.
Data ingestion lets you connect content from third-party platforms, local files, and databases.
Processing automatically parses and structures raw multi-modal data from various formats.
Enhancement transforms raw data for a more semantic knowledge-base using pluggable agents.
Vectorization generates semantic vector representations using various models like OpenAI or Cohere.
The Memory layer is where your enriched knowledge lives, ready to be retrieved.
Vector Storage stores embeddings in databases like Weaviate, Pinecone, or Qdrant.
File Storage persists raw and processed files using local storage or cloud options.
Media Serving allows access to media through Unbody’s CDN and signed URLs.
The Metadata Store keeps track of content structure, relationships, and context.
The Reasoning layer is where intelligence happens through decision-making and execution.
Text Generation offers built-in support for models like GPT-4 and Claude.
JSON Generation produces structured responses and machine-readable payloads.
Cloud-only support for visual image generation is on the roadmap.
Function Registry defines callable functions for agents via schema-based definitions.
Execution & Routing dynamically executes functions with intent parsing and argument validation.
The Action layer is where the backend connects to the outside world via APIs.
Content API allows querying your knowledge-base via GraphQL with filtering.
Push API pushes structured data directly into Unbody.
Admin API configures schemas, projects, pipelines, and permissions.
MCP connects Unbody to external systems, events, and workflows.
SDKs are available in TypeScript, iOS, and Android.
It supports chat endpoints with memory and long-term context.
The system includes integration with observability monitoring systems.
But for now, we’re in feedback mode and want to know what works and what breaks.
We are releasing the alpha because we wanted to build with the community feedback.
Link to the GitHub Repo.

title: The End of the Container Era: Apps Are a Historical Glitch
author: amir
blurb: Software containers are a historical glitch that force us to act as 'human routers' connecting disconnected apps. It's time to move beyond the 'Page Era' to an architecture built on pure intent.

summary.summary: We accept the friction and scattered attention of modern digital work because we lack a name for it.
This fatigue is not normal work but a symptom of a specific architectural failure.
We wrongly assume that apps and websites are the natural laws of software.
Software containers are a historical glitch properly attributed to macro-level constraints on building and shipping.
Distribution methods like floppy disks and SaaS domains forced software into standalone packages.
Vendors required a way to ship one static interface to millions of users from a server.
These logistical hurdles created rigid software boxes that force users to hop between them.
The resulting system is built on three pillars that are fundamentally anti-human.
In the digital world, unlike the physical one, you must travel to the tool.
Users must go to specific locations like Gmail or Salesforce to perform distinct actions.
Because these walled gardens don't talk to each other, users visit disconnected rooms repeatedly.
This physical separation of tools creates a deeper cognitive fracture.
Research from the project Re highlights that we remain trapped in the 'Page Era'.
The Page is a centralized model where the server defines the container top-down.
Humans naturally explore chunk-by-chunk rather than thinking in pre-defined Pages.
The OS forces users to translate their intent into its rigid language of launching containers.
Visualizing the disconnect shows how servers ship Pages while the human mind follows Threads.
Tabs are the ultimate symptom of an OS that fails to understand the thread of your work.
We pay a price because the logic is siloed and the software abstraction is wrong.
You become the human router manually copying context between boxes that don't communicate.
The result is a workflow defined by open tabs and infinite micro-searches.
This tax is paid with your attention, time, and nervous system.
The energy in the builder community suggests the dam is finally breaking on this issue.
Innovators like Naval Ravikant and AGI Inc are proving the future is about pure intent, not menus.
Teams like Zo and Wabi AI are exploring browser-native clouds and personal software fitting the user.
We are circling the truth that the use of software is the bottleneck, not the build.
A tweet visualizes the consensus that software interaction is the current bottleneck.
We must rethink architecture so the app doesn't exist, rather than just using agents to drive them.
This article is Part 1 of a series that will introduce the 'Faceless Data Layer'.
The team is currently cooking up something in stealth that tackles this architecture problem.

title: "AI-native" v.s. "AI-forced"
author: amir
blurb: The shift toward AI-native applications marks a fundamental change in how software is designed, yet current tools often feel "AI-forced" with fragmented toolchains. This post explores how merging AI and product stacks creates a cohesive foundation where AI is essential rather than just an add-on.

summary.summary: The shift toward AI-native applications marks a fundamental change in how software is designed, moving beyond AI-enabled features to where AI is the foundation.
Current AI tools often feel "AI-forced" rather than truly AI-native, creating a gap between advanced machine learning strides and actual product development.
A visual representation of the problem of AI-forced development.
The issue lies in how these tools impose a fragmented toolchain that feels clunky and forces developers into a parallel ecosystem.
This image illustrates the fragmented toolchain of AI-forced development in practice.
Dual systems for product data versus embeddings lead to data sync headaches and redundant management.
Separate API layers for product and AI functions mean double the endpoints to create, maintain, and secure.
Different ETL pipelines for product data vs. AI embeddings or features add unnecessary workflow complexity.
Duplicated cache setups for product data and model responses increase infrastructure load and maintenance.
Distinct CDNs for product assets vs. AI models and datasets drive up costs and deployment complexity.
Splitting logs between product and AI metrics creates gaps in monitoring and makes it hard to get a complete performance picture.
Different access requirements for product features vs. AI models mean more friction and a heavier security load.
Handling model inference errors separately from regular product errors adds an extra layer of exception management.
Product and model deployments require separate pipelines, complicating releases and increasing coordination work.
Product changes and AI experiments need separate tracking setups, making rollbacks and updates twice as complicated.
Dual backup systems for product data and AI embeddings add storage overhead and complicate recovery.
Separate infrastructure needs for product CPU and model GPU make scaling expensive and add management overhead.
The sheer duplication and disconnect in tooling is the real barrier to building AI-native applications right now.

title: AI is Complex, Do Not Try This In-House
author: amir

summary.summary: More founders are waking up to the fact that AI isn’t optional anymore but mandatory because users want answers instantly.
This image illustrates that AI is a necessity for modern SaaS products.
If you are thinking about integrating AI, you have probably heard about RAG, which is at the heart of most AI implementations.
We need our own perplexity to handle complex queries by diving deep into specific data sets, which is RAG in action.
We need our own ChatGPT tailored for our customer data to deliver spot-on answers unique to the business.
We need an autopilot for our documentation to save time by pulling the right information from databases, Google Drive, and Slack.
RAG is simply ChatGPT applied to your custom data to generate responses based on that data.
As a founder, I feel obliged to share two catches with you regarding RAG.
RAG alone won’t give you a complete product.
These aren’t challenges you want to tackle in-house without serious expertise and resources.
This diagram shows the 12 modules required to build a RAG system in-house.
Building a RAG system is a beast that involves 12 different modules, each with its own set of challenges.
Data Integration requires live updates every time your data sources get updated, which is one of the most annoying and complex tasks.
Data Processing is absolutely necessary work to format and chunk data to make it usable for AI.
Vectorization and Storage involves setting up and maintaining a vector database, which is a significant time sink.

title: Managing the UI state for generative data flow
author: amir
blurb: Moving from CRUD to generative AI requires a fundamental shift in mental models for UI state management. This guide explores why traditional patterns fail and how to build adaptive, context-aware interfaces for streaming and multi-stage generative flows.

summary.summary: While wiring up the UI for a basic agentic RAG layer, the entire model for state felt incompatible distinct from normal fetch/response flows.
The problem wasn't the code or async bugs, but the mental model of thinking like CRUD developers.
This post explains the conceptual foundation of what makes UI state management for generative flows different.
Before talking about managing it, the concept needs to be defined.
Generative data differs from database output as it is produced on the fly by a model, including text, images, and RAG responses.
The discussion remains grounded by using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as the main example.
To make this clearer, it helps to contrast it with the CRUD model.
An image compares generative data against CRUD data.
RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation, a pattern combining user questions with relevant data to generate a response.
An image illustrates the RAG flow involving retrieval, generation, and response.
The first step is to retrieve relevant content from data sources.
The second step is to generate an answer using that retrieved content as context.
This setup grounds generation in real context, helping the model answer using actual data.
This flow serves as the working example for the rest of the post.
In CRUD flows, you ask for a specific thing and get a complete fact back.
In generative flows, you get a generated response that is an interpretation built in real time.
That distinction leads to three fundamental differences in how we need to think about state.
A CRUD request is typically atomic, involving one request and one response.
An image depicts the atomic nature of a CRUD request and response.
In RAG and most gen workflows, the process is multi-step with at least two stages.
An image shows a minimal multi-stage pipeline of retrieving then generating.
A more realistic setup might include additional steps beyond the minimal case.
An image illustrates a realistic multi-stage generative pipeline.
Because stages can fail independently or stream results, a single loading flag breaks immediately.
In gen flows, the payload streams in over time, often token by token, unlike CRUD.
This stream can be sequential, non-monotonic, or involve refinement like diffusion.
If you're not thinking in terms of partial state and streaming updates, you'll overwrite your UI or show nothing.
An image compares parcel delivery to streaming token-by-token output.
A simplified example shows how gen output handling works in practice.
You build the data as it arrives instead of getting it all at once.
When you fetch a row in CRUD flows, the data is a precise and complete fact.
An image contrasts CRUD returning facts versus generative returning interpretations.
Generative responses are interpretations shaped by input, context, and probabilistic behavior.
Even when grounded with the same input data, the output can vary slightly every time.
In generative systems, the response is a version of the truth, unlike the truth in CRUD.
That distinction changes what you can assume about output predictability and UI treatment.
Once you understand generative data is multi-stage and interpretative, state management must change.
Generative outputs like text return a readable stream of tokens rather than all at once.
Instead of setting the final result, you append tokens as they arrive.
You also need to support canceling the stream immediately to save money and handle user changes.
An image illustrating streaming with append and cancel support.
Without cancel support, you will burn tokens unnecessarily.
Without append logic, you cannot reflect progress in the UI.
The second key takeaway is that context is the real state you need to manage.
The UI is reacting to a pipeline where the composition of stages is called context.
Context should be treated as a first-class application state object rather than a one-off response.
An example shows what a structured context might look like in a RAG system.
An image depicts a sample context structure for a RAG system.
A typical mistake is discarding the intermediate states and retrieved records that made output possible.
Discarding context essentially throws away the trace of your reasoning.
This context object is the actual state of your generative UI.
From a frontend perspective, the component should be bound to the context of what the model saw.
When users regenerate or edit, this context is your truth, not just the output.
The context becomes a contract between the system and the user effectively.
The system presents the output as the best interpretation given a specific context.
This rationale makes it easier to justify or explain why the model said something.
Understanding generation as a pipeline shifts how you model state in the UI.
In a gen flow with multiple steps, a simple loading flag is insufficient.
Your app needs to treat each stage as its own state machine.
Union types guarantee that the system is never in conflicting states like loading and done.
You can give precise feedback to the user regarding retrieval or generation progress.
You can retry only part of the flow, such as generation, if retrieval was fine.
Your UI logic becomes much easier to manage when you switch on state.
In generative flows, retries are a feature rather than just for network failures.
Sometimes you simply want a second version or the model failed to produce valid output.
Because every stage is separate, retries should also be stage-aware.
An image displays a stage-aware retry flow in generative pipelines.
Managing UI state for generative data involves tracking context and reflecting actual pipeline stages.
This applies if you are working with RAG, calling OpenAI functions, or chaining LLM tools.
A follow-up post purely on engineering mechanics like hooks and stores is being considered.
Feedback is welcomed from those building generative features and thinking about developer ergonomics.

title: AI in 2023: Paradoxical Advancement
author: amir
blurb: As 2023 ends, we reflect on the paradox between massive technological AI leaps and their surprising underutilization in practical business applications. This post explores the gaps in law, healthcare, and publishing while proposing a low-code path to democratization.

summary.summary: This section frames the discussion on bridging the increasing gap between AI as tech and its applications.
As 2023 draws to a close, a critical observation emerges regarding the stark contrast between technological leaps and real-world applications in the business sector.
Despite being at the forefront of a technological revolution, AI's potential to transform passive data into actionable knowledge remains largely untapped.
This header introduces examples of untapped AI potential in industries.
We dive into specific industry scenarios to highlight how AI's transformative potential remains largely untapped.
In law firms, AI applications like automated case research are rarely seen in practice.
Adoption in healthcare is sporadic and largely confined to experimental segments rather than widespread clinical practice.
The publishing industry continues to rely heavily on traditional methods, with AI-driven innovations being more of an exception than the norm.
These examples underscore a significant gap where practical application is still in its nascent stages.
The complexity of AI technology is a significant factor contributing to its limited application in business.
Technologically sophisticated tools frequently necessitate specialized knowledge to operate, presenting a barrier to their widespread adoption.
To truly harness AI's potential, we need input from a broader range of professionals like creative minds and business strategists.
Unbody was created as a low-code privacy-friendly platform to democratize AI technology and simplify AI tools.
We are ready to explore ways we can help law firms, publishers, and businesses use AI to analyze files and enhance customer experience.
The key to unlocking AI's full potential in business lies in bridging the gap between its technological capabilities and practical applications.

title: From Query to Context: Building Agentic RAG with Unbody's JSON Endpoint
author: amir
blurb: Learn how to upgrade from naive retrieval to Agentic RAG by parsing nuanced user queries into structured parameters using Unbody's generative JSON endpoint. this guide walks through using Zod schemas to extract precise search filters and constraints.

summary.summary: I recently spoke at AI Thinkers Abu Dhabi about building robust RAG systems, noting that a naive approach often isn't enough for nuanced queries.
This chunk presents a user quote asking for an Italian dish for two people without sausage, ready in under 30 minutes.
Agentic RAG comes in to parsing the query into structured parameters like "no sausage" or "Italian dish" for more precise retrieval.
Let’s see how to do this with Unbody—step by step.
You need a Unbody project set up with your data, such as a collection of recipes, already ingested and indexed.
You have your API key and Project ID from the Unbody dashboard to proceed.
If you haven’t set this up yet, check out the Unbody docs for a quick start on creating a project and uploading your data.
Now you can start calling Unbody’s APIs to search, filter, and generate.
Knowing the schema tells us exactly which parameters we can extract from a user’s query when working with our data.
Knowing these fields lets us decide which parts of the user’s query should be parsed and parameterized.
The user states they want an Italian dish with no sausage and ready in under 30 minutes.
For that query, we know to extract the concept, ingredients to exclude, and a time constraint.
RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation and consists of two main parts: Retrieval and Generation.
Take the user’s entire query directly as the first step in a naive approach.
Feed the top documents from that retrieval into a text-generation prompt.
The system doesn’t actually understand the user’s intention, just trying to match text semantically, which leads to irrelevant results.
The agentic way is to parse the user’s query into structured parameters first.
Apply filters to our knowledge base such as "exclude sausage" or "max 30 minutes."
Generate the final response using only the truly relevant documents gathered from filtering.
The general syntax we will be using is going to be with Unbdoy’s chain syntax methods.
To translate this into a proper RAG query, we need to extract three specific pieces of information.
We extract main keywords or concepts from the user's query to apply to semantic search.
We identify any specific filters to pass to the where function.
We identify the prompt or task description for the generate task.
To do this, we will be using Unbody’s generative JSON endpoint which utilize the Zod library under the hood.
Unbody’s generative JSON receives two arguments: a set of messages with role definition and a zod schema.
In Zod schema basically we can define what the shape of generative json should be like, starting with the concepts field.
We’re expecting an array of strings or null if nothing is extracted.
The describe method adds a note so that anyone reading the code knows that this field represents the main search terms.
Next, we need to capture ingredients that the user wants to include in the same way.
The description clarifies that this field is for ingredients the user explicitly wants in the recipe.
Now, let’s expand our schema by adding all the fields we expect from the query.
We add an includeCuisineTypes field for preferred cuisine types.
We add a totalTimeMinutesMax field for a maximum time constraint.
Here’s the full Zod schema with descriptions for every field provided.
Now that our schema is complete, lets create a function called queryParser and integrate the entire logic into it.
We pass our complete querySchema to the generative endpoint within the function.
The system message instructs the model to analyze the query provided.
The returned payload gives us a well-structured object containing all the extracted parameters.
In this snippet, the model processes the user’s input and returns a structured JSON object.
Now that we’ve parsed the query into detailed parameters, it’s time to build the final RAG pipeline consisting of three parts.
We want to search based on the main concepts extracted, or fallback to the full query if the array is empty.
This snippet ensures that our semantic search is as focused as possible by prioritizing specific keywords.
Now comes the slightly more complex part: turning each extracted filter into a proper "where" clause.
If the query has an includeIngredients array, we want to add a filter for it.
We only want to add this filter when includeIngredients exists using a conditional.
If includeIngredients exists, we include the filter; if not, we simply add an empty array.
Next, if the query specifies ingredients to exclude like "no sausage," we want to add a filter for each item.
Each ingredient that should be excluded is mapped into a NotEqual filter, conditionally adding them only if they exist.
We are combining All Filters Using the And Operator.
Finally, we combine all these filters into a single query.
This final combined filter checks each parameter and only adds a condition if that parameter exists.
We are generating the final answer with the generate fromMany method.
After we’ve retrieved and filtered our documents, we use the generation step to produce a final, coherent answer.
The system message instructs the model to consider the retrieved results when generating the response.
This section covers bringing it all together into the complete RAG pipeline.
Here’s what the full API handler might look like, such as in a Next.js project.
The user’s free-form query is processed by parseQuery to return a structured object with parameters.
Semantic Search focuses on the extracted concepts found in the parsed object.
Filtering applies each filter conditionally using the And operator.
Limiting via autocut keeps our result set manageable.
Finally, the generate fromMany function produces a coherent answer that integrates the retrieved documents.
Check out the full demo of this Agentic RAG system in action on YouTube.
Interested in digging into the code, you can find the complete source code on GitHub.
The link goes to the unbody-io example-next.js repository tree for recipes.
With Unbody’s Agentic RAG approach, you’re capturing intention and filtering precisely rather than just matching keywords.

Experiment with the sample code and start tailoring your own Agentic RAG pipeline.
Check out the Unbody documentation for further insights and advanced use cases.
We’d love to see what you create, so share your projects on our community forums or social channels.
Consider joining our open-source community to help shape the future of intelligent applications.
Happy building, and let’s push the boundaries of what our applications can do together!

title: What the F**k is an AI-native app?
author: amir
blurb: AI-first is becoming the new mobile-first, but what defines a truly AI-native application? This post explores the transition to human-centric software, the pillars of personalization and context, and how to build complex AI stacks without starting from scratch.

summary.summary: AI-first is becoming the new mobile-first, and this post dives into the characteristics of AI-native apps.
The prevalence of large language models necessitates a shift in software design towards an "AI-first" mindset similar to how "mobile-first" transformed the industry.
An AI-native app is defined as more human software that understands us and can adapt to humans.
The first step towards human-like software is its ability to adapt and tailor to our individual needs and contexts, such as the difference between work and home environments.
For example, a chatbot at work must understand your specific company, department, and team to effectively search documents.
Software needs access to the diverse data footprints we produce daily to provide a personalized user experience.
Traditionally, managing data for apps involves using a CMS, which often requires considerable manual effort like copying, pasting, and content analysis.
Image illustrating traditional versus AI-native data management for personalization.
Conventionally, creating structured data for platforms requires re-curating existing content like PDFs and Docs and manually applying SEO tags and keywords.
AI-native applications bypass traditional steps by using AI to maintain data in its original format and location while adapting it to needs effectively.
This process requires the capability to aggregate and process documents, files, and data from all different locations and platforms.
The second crucial aspect is context, utilizing the interconnected nature of content to link data points rather than keeping them isolated.
Image illustrating context awareness through semantically connected data sources.
Context enriches content by connecting different "islands" of information, such as linking technical documentation to related community discussions on Slack or GitHub.
Semantically connecting topics through advanced features like "semantic search" allows for a deeper understanding beyond simple keyword matching.
With the rise of AI, users now expect to communicate with apps through conversation rather than just seeking information.
Image showing the shift from information seeking to conversational interaction with software.
The preference for natural human language requires apps to understand and respond in human language through deeper semantic analysis.
To support interactive approaches, features like generative search, image captioning, and chatbots are essential for developing AI-native apps.
Image showing the technical breakdown of AI-native app components.
The technology that makes an app AI-first is broken down into three essential main areas.
Data Aggregation is all about getting data from different places and making sure it syncs up nicely.
Data Processing includes tasks like cleaning data, chunking, and vectorizing to turn raw data into designated AI-ready data.
The functions division borrows from RAG but goes beyond it to define actions without getting too technical.
Data Retrieval acts as a supercharged search engine inside your app to help you find exactly what you need quickly.
Data Augmentation involves making existing data better by adding details or tweaking it to understand scenarios better.
Data Generation goes beyond retrieval to create new bits of content on the spot based on what users are asking for.
Assembling a system that can handle these components is complex, as shown in the following visual.
Image showing the complexity of assembling a full AI-native system from scratch.
Building this system requires familiarity with Python and integrating about ten components ranging from document parsers to LLM APIs.
Beyond AI elements, real-world apps require CDNs, video hosting, and image processing to ensure performance across platforms.
Unbody is an AI-as-a-service platform that automates the entire AI development pipeline to solve these challenges for developers.
Image illustrating how Unbody simplifies AI-native app development.
Unbody automates the aggregation and processing of data from any source and format, from Google Drive to local folders.
The platform streamlines AI model management by handling upgrades and deployments for models from providers like OpenAI and Hugging Face.
Unbody makes integrating AI functionalities into apps as simple as writing a single line of code via its API or SDKs.
Video demonstrating a short Javascript semantic search implementation.
Just connect your data, select your AI stack, and start building with just one line of code.
